paragraphs.heading: Gravity as geometry
paragraphs.text: General relativity is Albert Einstein's theory of gravity, published in May 1916, and it is how modern physics describes gravity for large objects. It treats gravity as a feature of the geometry of space and time, joined into one four-dimensional whole called spacetime. Spacetime can curve, and the amount of curving is tied to the energy, momentum and stress of whatever is there, matter and radiation included. A set of equations, the Einstein field equations, spells out that link.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond Newton
paragraphs.text: The physicist John Archibald Wheeler summed up the idea in one line: spacetime tells matter how to move, while matter tells spacetime how to curve. Newton's law of gravity can be seen as what general relativity predicts when spacetime is almost flat around masses that stay still. But Einstein's theory also makes predictions that Newton's law does not. They concern the flow of time, the geometry of space, the motion of falling bodies and the path of light.

paragraphs.heading: What the theory predicts
paragraphs.text: Those predictions include black holes, singularities and the Shapiro time delay, as well as the slowing of time by gravity, the gravitational redshift of light, and gravitational lensing. A black hole is a region where space and time are bent so far that nothing, not even light, can get out. Gravitational lensing is the bending of light that turns one distant object into warped and repeated images. The theory also predicts gravitational waves, which LIGO and other observatories have now detected directly. Every test of the theory so far has agreed with it.

paragraphs.heading: Eight years of work
paragraphs.text: Einstein started in 1907 from a simple thought experiment about an observer falling freely, and spent eight years looking for a theory of gravity that fit with relativity. After many detours and false starts, he presented the Einstein field equations to the Prussian Academy of Science in November 1915. The mathematics he needed came from Riemannian geometry, a kind of non-Euclidean geometry. The mathematician Marcel Grossmann pointed this out, and he and Einstein published it in 1913.

paragraphs.heading: Black holes and the universe
paragraphs.text: The field equations are hard to solve, but in 1916 Karl Schwarzschild found the first exact non-trivial solution, now called the Schwarzschild metric. It became the groundwork for describing the last stages of collapse and the objects we now call black holes. In 1917 Einstein applied the theory to the whole universe, assumed it was static, and added a new term, the cosmological constant, to match that assumption. By 1929, though, work by Hubble and others showed an expanding universe, which fits solutions Friedmann had found in 1922 without that term. Lemaître used them for the earliest Big Bang models, and Einstein later called the constant the biggest blunder of his life.

paragraphs.heading: From curiosity to mainstream
paragraphs.text: For a while the theory was something of a curiosity, even though it fit special relativity and explained effects Newton's gravity could not. In 1915 Einstein showed that it accounted for the puzzling shift in Mercury's orbit with no fudge factors. In 1919 an expedition led by Eddington confirmed its prediction that the Sun bends starlight, seen during the total eclipse of 29 May, and Einstein became famous at once. Still, it only joined mainstream physics in its golden age, roughly 1960 to 1975, when physicists came to understand black holes and linked them to quasars.

paragraphs.heading: What is still open
paragraphs.text: Solutions of the theory that change over time let us trace the history of the universe backward and forward. That made general relativity the framework of modern cosmology and led to the discovery of the Big Bang and the cosmic microwave background. Despite many rival theories, it remains the simplest one that fits the experimental data. What it does not do is fit with quantum physics: nobody has found a self-consistent theory of quantum gravity, and nobody yet knows how gravity unites with the strong, weak and electromagnetic forces.
